full_judgment:
7. Mr. Bishwdeb Chokroborty the learned Advocate along with Mr. S. M. Zafar Sadeque for the pre-emptor-opposite parties, on the other hand, vehemently contends that the pre-emptee petitioners were required in law to raise specific objection with regard to defect the parties by giving necessary particulars of the remaining co-sharer tenants in the disputed khatian at the earliest opportunity which they filed to do. The learned Advocate referring the judgments of the Courts below submits. that both the Courts below on assigning sound reasons concurrently held that all the necessary parties having been properly impleaded in the pre-emption application and the application for pre-emption was filed within 4 (four) months from the date of knowledge of the disputed transfer and as such the grievance of the learned Advocate for the petitioner appears to have no substance. The learned advocate lastly submits that there is no reliable evidence at all on record that the case land is being used as a homestead of the pre-emptee petitioner.; and thereby the learned appellate Court bellow did not commit any error of law in affirming the judgment and order of the trial Court and hence the rule is liable to be discharged. 

 8. I have gone through the judgments of the Courts below and also had the opportunity of examining the entire evidence of P. W. an O.P.Ws 1-2. It appears that the deed of transfer was registered on 16.09.1996 and the application for pre-emption having been filed on 30.11.1996 i.e. within the statuary period of limitation, provided in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 and the lower appellate Court as well as the trial Court upon consideration of the evidence on record having rightly held that the Case was not barred by limitation. It also appears from the findings of the Courts below that there was no defect of parties inasmuch as there was no specific objection with regard to defect the parties by giving necessary particulars of the remaining co-sharer tenants in the disputed khatian at the earliest opportunity. On this point the finding of the learned Senior Assistant Judge is quoted below:- 

 As already indicated above, Nurul Islam is a co-sharer in Plot No. 2085, which is included in the khatian constituting the holding transferred. The learned Munsif's view on this point is quoted below:- 

 "But the OPs. contend that their father Nurul Islam is the owner of the disputed plot No. 2085 by inheritance. But co-owner ship of a disputed plot without being a co-sharer in the khatian do not confer any right to the co-owner of the plot to resist the pre-emption". 

 This view clearly shows that the learned Munsif misconceived as to what is meant by the expression "co-sherer in the holding". When Nurul Islam was a co-sharer in one of the plots of khatian he was certainly a co-sharer in the holding. But failure of the pre-emptors to implead him in the application for pre-emption is a serious defect of party since impleading of a co-sharer, whether by inheritance or by purchase, is a mandatory provision of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The application for pre-emption is therefore liable to be dismissed, as has been rightly held by the appellate Court. This omission was pointed out at the earliest point of time but the omission was not supplied. In the circumstances, the impugned order of the High Court Division restoring the trial Court's order allowing pre-emption is not sustainable in law.
